seo.title: 36 Vet and Pet Logos Explained
seo.description: 36 veterinary and pet logos explained by a brand designer: vet clinics like Banfield and VCA, animal health brands like Zoetis and Royal Canin, plus the best dog and cat brand logos.

intro:
The best veterinary logos mix care with warmth. A vet has to look as trustworthy as a doctor, but the patients are dogs and cats, so the strongest logos add one friendly animal detail to a clean, medical-looking base: the pets inside Banfield's cross, the cat face hidden in Thrive's v, or the heart-shaped pet in Bond Vet's mark.

What makes a good veterinary logo?

Trust first: owners bring a family member to the vet, so clear type, calm colours and a simple layout matter more than a clever drawing.

One animal detail: a paw, an ear or a pet face tells people what you do at a glance. Use one, not a whole zoo.

A colour you can own: most clinics pick blue or green. Coral, orange, purple or brown, like Bond Vet, Banfield or Modern Animal, makes a practice easier to remember.

Room to grow: the logo has to work on a clinic sign, scrubs, an app icon and a pet insurance card.

Below are 36 logos in four groups: vet clinics and animal hospitals, animal health and pet insurance companies, dog brands and cat brands. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. For more ideas, see my guides to animal symbolism in logo design, brand mascots and healthcare logos.

logoResearch.name: Banfield Pet Hospital
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Banfield was founded in Portland, Oregon, in 1955 and is now part of Mars Veterinary Health.
observations: An orange medical cross has a dog and a cat cut into it, so the symbol says both care and pets.
The name sits over two lines, with Banfield in teal and "Pet Hospital" in grey capitals.

logoResearch.name: VCA Animal Hospitals
logoResearch.verifiedFact: VCA was founded in Los Angeles in 1986 and is now owned by Mars.
observations: Heavy navy lowercase letters make the three initials the main part of the logo.
A small cluster of purple, teal and coral diamonds adds colour and works as a friendly symbol.

logoResearch.name: BluePearl Pet Hospital
logoResearch.verifiedFact: BluePearl was founded in Tampa, Florida, in 1996 and runs specialty and emergency animal hospitals.
observations: A short blue swoosh sits on the B like a tick, the only symbol in the logo.
A two-line wordmark in navy and bright blue keeps the long name compact.

logoResearch.name: Thrive Pet Healthcare
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pathway Vet Alliance renamed itself Thrive Pet Healthcare in 2022.
observations: The v in the name is drawn as a green pet face with two ears, a clever hidden symbol.
Bright blue lowercase letters and a green tagline line make the brand feel optimistic.

logoResearch.name: Bond Vet
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bond Vet was founded in New York in 2018 and runs urgent and primary care clinics.
observations: A coral heart shape doubles as a pet face with two pointed ears.
Navy and coral split the name in two, so Bond and Vet read as separate words.

logoResearch.name: Small Door Veterinary
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Small Door opened its first practice in Manhattan in 2019 as a membership-based vet.
observations: A rounded, friendly serif in lowercase sets the name like a boutique hotel.
"Veterinary" is set in tiny, widely spaced capitals underneath, almost like a tagline.

logoResearch.name: Modern Animal
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Modern Animal was founded in Los Angeles in 2018 as a membership-based vet clinic.
observations: A heavy serif in dark brown feels warm and premium rather than clinical.
Small spaced capitals for "Veterinary Care" sit underneath, so the brand name leads.

logoResearch.name: Medivet
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Medivet was founded in 1987 and runs hundreds of vet practices across the UK.
observations: A small pink M above the name hides a pet's face, with ears at the top and a nose in the middle.
Blue lettering and the line "& Partners" show that local vets co-own the practices.

logoResearch.name: Vets4Pets
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Vets4Pets is a UK chain of vet practices owned by Pets at Home.
observations: Two greens split the name, with dark green for Vets and bright green for Pets.
A small, light "for" replaces the 4, which makes the name easy to read aloud.

logoResearch.name: Zoetis
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Zoetis was spun off from Pfizer in 2013 and is the world's largest animal health company.
observations: Bright orange lowercase letters make the brand feel friendly for a pharmaceutical company.
The z has a looping tail, a small flourish that gives the wordmark its own character.

logoResearch.name: Elanco
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Elanco began as an agricultural division of Eli Lilly and became an independent company in 2019.
observations: White italic letters sit inside a blue box that slants upward.
The slanted box suggests forward movement and works as a compact badge on packs.

logoResearch.name: IDEXX
logoResearch.verifiedFact: IDEXX was founded in Maine in 1983 and makes diagnostic tests and lab equipment for vets.
observations: Heavy black capitals have small cuts in the letters, which makes them look engineered.
"Laboratories" is spaced wide underneath, matching the width of the name.

logoResearch.name: Covetrus
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Covetrus was formed in 2019 by combining Henry Schein Animal Health and Vets First Choice.
observations: Navy lowercase letters keep the made-up name readable and calm.
A folded ribbon in red, navy and teal adds colour at the end of the name.

logoResearch.name: Merck Animal Health
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Merck Animal Health is known as MSD Animal Health outside the United States and Canada.
observations: The teal Merck symbol of circles and shapes is shared with the human health business.
"Animal Health" sits under MERCK in a lighter weight to separate the division from the parent.

logoResearch.name: Hill's Pet Nutrition
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hill's is based in Topeka, Kansas, and has been owned by Colgate-Palmolive since 1976.
observations: A red and navy H with a white swoosh looks like a flag and gives the brand a strong symbol.
A heavy serif sets Hill's under the mark, giving the brand a classic, trustworthy tone.

logoResearch.name: Royal Canin
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Royal Canin was founded in France in 1968 by vet Jean Cathary and has been owned by Mars since 2001.
observations: A red crown made of dots sits above the name and hints at the royal in the name.
Bold red capitals make the logo stand out on shelves and in vet clinics.

logoResearch.name: ManyPets
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The London-based insurer Bought By Many renamed itself ManyPets in 2021.
observations: Dark green letters with rounded ends look soft and approachable.
Joining the two words with a capital P keeps the name short and easy to read.

logoResearch.name: Pumpkin
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pumpkin is a New York pet insurer founded in 2019.
observations: Heavy, wide capitals in dark plum look bold and confident.
There is no symbol or orange, so the friendly name does all the work.

logoResearch.name: BarkBox
logoResearch.verifiedFact: BarkBox launched in New York in 2012, and its parent company now uses the name BARK.
observations: Heavy black capitals look like they were cut from paper.
Three short lines after the K look like a bark or a wagging tail.

logoResearch.name: Rover
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Rover was founded in Seattle in 2011 and connects dog owners with sitters and walkers.
observations: A green paw print sits before the name and works as the app icon.
A bold, slanted script makes the wordmark feel lively and friendly.

logoResearch.name: Wag!
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Wag! was founded in 2015 and lets owners book dog walkers through an app.
observations: Very heavy green letters fill the space and are easy to read on small screens.
The exclamation mark is part of the name and adds energy.

logoResearch.name: The Farmer's Dog
logoResearch.verifiedFact: The Farmer's Dog was founded in New York in 2014 and delivers fresh dog food.
observations: Hand-drawn white lettering sits inside a round coral badge.
The badge looks like a food label or a stamp, which fits a fresh food brand.

logoResearch.name: Ollie
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ollie was founded in New York in 2016 and delivers fresh dog food.
observations: Heavy, condensed black letters fill the logo with no symbol.
The tall letters make the short name feel bold and modern.

logoResearch.name: Pedigree
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Pedigree is one of the biggest dog food brands owned by Mars.
observations: A blue show rosette sits behind the name, a nod to prize-winning dogs.
White slab-serif letters are designed for the brand's yellow packs, so the logo needs a coloured background.

logoResearch.name: Milk-Bone
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Milk-Bone biscuits were first made in New York in 1908.
observations: The logo sits inside a bone shape, so the product and the brand are the same picture.
A small red heart replaces the hyphen between Milk and Bone.

logoResearch.name: Fi
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Fi was founded in New York in 2017 and makes GPS collars for dogs.
observations: Just two black italic letters make one of the shortest logos in the list.
The heavy slant gives the two letters a sense of speed, which suits a tracking device.

logoResearch.name: KONG
logoResearch.verifiedFact: KONG was founded in Colorado in 1976 and is known for its rubber dog toys.
observations: Heavy red capitals are tightly spaced like a toy brand.
The red toy shape at the end of the name is the product itself.

logoResearch.name: Whiskas
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Whiskas is a Mars cat food brand that has been sold in the UK since 1958.
observations: White lowercase letters sit inside a bright purple box.
A darker purple cat's head with two pointed ears is drawn behind the name.

logoResearch.name: Meow Mix
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Meow Mix was launched in 1974.
observations: Bouncy, uneven letters look like they are moving to the brand's jingle.
Orange-red letters are stacked on two lines, which makes the logo compact on packs.

logoResearch.name: Friskies
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Friskies is one of Nestlé Purina's best-known cat food brands.
observations: Red letters with a yellow outline sit on a yellow banner.
A small Purina badge and the line "Feed The Senses" connect it to its parent brand.

logoResearch.name: Sheba
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Sheba is a Mars cat food brand sold in small trays and pouches.
observations: A gold shield gives the brand a luxury feel, with a small black cat sitting on top of the S.
A thin script name runs across the shield like a signature.

logoResearch.name: 9Lives
logoResearch.verifiedFact: 9Lives was launched in 1959, and Morris the Cat has been its mascot since 1969.
observations: A big 9 turns into the script word Lives.
Curved lines of small text, "Caring for cats" and "Since 1959", frame the name like a badge.

logoResearch.name: Temptations
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Temptations is a cat treat brand owned by Mars.
observations: A thick yellow outline wraps the name like a speech bubble.
Black italic letters make the name look fun and playful.

logoResearch.name: Felix
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Felix is a Nestlé Purina cat food brand that was relaunched in the UK in 1989 with its black and white cat mascot.
observations: Black lowercase script letters look like they were written with a brush.
Red paw prints over the x and a small Purina badge complete the logo.

logoResearch.name: Smalls
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Smalls was founded in New York in 2017 and delivers fresh cat food.
observations: Thin, wide capitals are spaced far apart and look like a fashion brand.
With no symbol or colour, the logo feels premium rather than cute.

logoResearch.name: Litter-Robot
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Litter-Robot was created in Michigan in 2000 and is now made by Whisker.
observations: A dot replaces the hyphen in the name, like a small piece of technology.
The line "by whisker" underneath shows the parent brand.

listIntro: The boards below show all 36 logos in one consistent format, grouped into vet clinics, animal health and pet insurance, dog brands and cat brands.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the quality of the care, food or products behind it.
sectionIntroductions: Vet clinic logos balance medical trust with pet warmth. The big hospital groups use crosses and clear wordmarks, while newer clinics like Bond Vet, Small Door and Modern Animal look more like lifestyle brands.
Animal health companies sell to vets and farmers, so their logos look like pharmaceutical brands. Pet food and pet insurance brands talk to owners and use warmer colours and softer letters.
Dog brands are loud and playful. Heavy letters, bright colours and one doggy detail, like a paw, a bone or a bark, do most of the work.
Cat brands lean on cat ears, scripts and premium cues like gold and purple, while newer brands like Smalls and Litter-Robot use clean, modern wordmarks.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of veterinary and pet logos, not a ranking of clinics, insurers or products.
Look at how each logo uses type, colour and one animal detail to signal care, fun or quality.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a clinic sign, a pet food pack and an app icon.

findings.heading: Hidden pets beat cartoon pets
findings.text: Banfield's cross, Thrive's v, Bond Vet's heart and Medivet's M hide an animal inside a simple shape. They feel friendly without looking childish.

findings.heading: New clinics look like lifestyle brands
findings.text: Small Door, Modern Animal and Bond Vet use serifs, brown, coral and lowercase letters, closer to a boutique hotel than a hospital.

findings.heading: Dog brands are loud
findings.text: BARK, Wag!, KONG, Ollie and Fi use very heavy letters and strong colours that read well on packs and small screens.

findings.heading: Cat brands go premium
findings.text: Sheba's gold shield, Whiskas' purple and Felix's brush script give cat food a softer, more indulgent feel.

findings.heading: Parents leave a mark
findings.text: Purina badges on Friskies and Felix, "by whisker" on Litter-Robot and "& Partners" on Medivet show who stands behind the brand.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a vet clinic logo
checklistItems: Does it look trustworthy enough for a medical service?
Is there one simple animal detail, not a whole collection of pets?
Does it work for dogs, cats and other animals, not just one species?
Is the colour different from the clinics near you?
Will it still read on a clinic sign, scrubs, a reminder text and an app icon?

faq.question: What makes a good veterinary logo?
faq.answer: A good veterinary logo looks trustworthy, friendly and simple. Most strong examples use a clear wordmark, one or two calm colours and one animal detail, such as a paw, an ear or a pet face hidden inside a shape.

faq.question: What colours are best for a vet clinic logo?
faq.answer: Blue and green are the most common because they feel calm and medical. To stand out, many newer clinics use coral, orange, purple or warm brown, like Bond Vet, Banfield and Modern Animal.

faq.question: Should a vet logo show a dog or a cat?
faq.answer: It can, but keep it simple and include both if you treat both. Many clinics use a neutral detail, like a paw, a heart or a pet face that could be either animal, so no pet owner feels left out.

faq.question: How is a pet brand logo different from a vet logo?
faq.answer: A vet logo has to feel safe and professional. A pet food, toy or accessory brand can be louder and more playful, with heavy letters, bright colours and humour, as BARK, KONG and Meow Mix show.

faq.question: How much does a veterinary logo cost?
faq.answer: Prices range from a few hundred dollars for a template to tens of thousands with a large agency. I design a complete brand identity in one week for a flat $3,000, including the logo, colours, typography and guidelines.
